entities.name: Almohad Caliphate
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Almohad Caliphate (al-Muwahhidun — 'Those who affirm Divine Unity'), founded in 1121 by Ibn Tumart in the Atlas Mountains of Morocco, was the last great Berber empire of North Africa and al-Andalus, ruling from the Atlantic to Tripolitania and from the Sahara to Toledo at its height (1150-1220). The Almohads produced medieval philosophy's two greatest minds — Averroes (Ibn Rushd) and Maimonides — while simultaneously conducting religious persecutions that forced both out of al-Andalus; this paradox defines the complexity of medieval Islamic cultural history.

Ibn Tumart, a Berber scholar who studied in Baghdad and returned preaching strict theological unitarianism, declared himself the Mahdi and began a religious reform movement from the Moroccan High Atlas. The Almohads overthrew the Almoravid Dynasty (itself a Berber empire) in 1147, then conquered al-Andalus, uniting North Africa and Spain under Berber rule for the first time. The Almohads' architectural legacy — the Giralda (Seville), Koutoubia Mosque (Marrakesh), and Hassan Tower (Rabat) — represents the apex of Berber-Islamic architecture.

Averroes (1126-1198), the court physician and philosopher who wrote commentaries on Aristotle so influential that European scholastics called Aristotle 'the Philosopher' and Averroes 'the Commentator,' and Maimonides (1135-1204), the greatest medieval Jewish philosopher, both lived and worked in Almohad Córdoba — before persecution drove them out, Averroes to exile, Maimonides to Egypt. The Almohads' forced conversion of Jews and Christians created the first mass refugee crisis in Iberian history.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Almohad Caliphate hosted Averroes and Maimonides — medieval philosophy's two greatest minds — while simultaneously persecuting them, and the Averroes commentaries transmitted to Latin Europe triggered the Scholastic revolution that produced Thomas Aquinas, the Renaissance, and ultimately Western science.
